children.html: Does gratitude always work? Ambivalence over emotional expression inhibits the beneficial effect of gratitude on well-being
Lung Hung Chen<sup>1</sup>, Mei-Yen Chen<sup>1</sup>, and Ying-Mei Tsai<sup>2</sup>
<sup>1</sup>Department of Recreation and Leisure Industry Management, National Taiwan Sport University, Taoyuan County, Taiwan

7 he psychological benefit of gratitude has been well demonstrated in previous studies. However, when we examined these studies closely, we found that the moderators were rarely investigated, suggesting that further work is needed to explore the boundaries of gratitude In this regard, the authors have proposed that ambivalence over emotional expression might be a potential moderator that would inhibit the beneficial effect of gratitude on well-being. Two studies were conducted to examine our hypothesis. Study 1 consisted of 353 Taiwanese college students who completed the Gratitude Questionnaire-Taiwan version (GQ-T), Ambivalence over Emotional Expression Questionnaire (AEQ), and one question about subjective happiness. We found that ambivalence over emotional expression significantly moderated the effect of gratitude on happiness. To validate our findings in Study 1, 233 Taiwanese college students were recruited for Study 2, and they completed the GQ-T, AEQ, subjective happiness short-form UCLA loneliness scale, as well as the Center for Epidemiological Studies Depression Scale (CES-D). Both studies demonstrated that ambivalence over emotional expression moderated the relationship between gratitude and well-being indexes. Simply stated, the authors found that across the two independent samples, among students who are high in ambivalence over emotional expression, the beneficial effect of gratitude on subjective happiness was inhibited. However, the moderating pattern for loneliness and depression was contrary to our expectations, indicating that high ambivalence over emotional expression does not inhibit gratitude. Possible explanations and implications for social relationships and emotional expression are discussed.
Keywords: Positive psychology; Affect trait; Altruism; Emotional conflicts.

7 l beneficio psicológico de la gratitud ha sido bien demostrado en estudios previos. Sin embargo, cuando examinamos de cerca estos estudios, encontramos que los moderadores rara vez han sido investigados, sugiriendo que se necesita seguir explorando los límites de la gratitud. En este sentido, los autores han propuesto que la ambivalencia en la expresión emocional puede ser un potencial moderador que inhibiría el efecto beneficioso de la gratitud en el bienestar. Se realizaron dos estudios para examinar nuestra hipótesis. El Estudio 1 consistió en que 353 estudiantes universitarios taiwaneses completaran el Cuestionario de Gratitud-versión taiwanesa (GQ-T, por sus siglas en inglés), un Cuestionario de Ambivalencia en la Expresión Emocional (AEQ), y una pregunta de felicidad subjetiva. Encontramos que la ambivalencia en la expresión emocional moderaba significativamente el efecto de la gratitud sobre la felicidad. A fin de validar los resultados del Estudio 1, se reclutaron 233 estudiantes universitarios taiwaneses para el Estudio 2, quienes completaron el GO-T, AEO, la felicidad subjetiva, la versión abreviada de la Escala de Soledad de UCLA, así como la Escala de Depresión del Centro de Estudios Epidemiológicos (CES -D). Ambos estudios demostraron consistentemente que la ambivalencia en la expresión emocional modera la relación entre los índices de gratitud y bienestar. En pocas palabras, los autores encontraron que en las dos muestras independientes, para los estudiantes con elevada ambivalencia en la expresión emocional, los efectos beneficiosos de la gratitud sobre la felicidad subjetiva están inhibidos. Sin embargo, el patrón de moderación de la soledad y la depresión fue contrario a nuestras expectativas, indicando que la elevada ambivalencia en la expresión emocional no inhibe la gratitud. Se discuten las posibles explicaciones e implicaciones para las relaciones sociales y la expresión emocional.

The beneficent effect of gratitude on well-being has interested psychologists for some time (McCullough, Kilpatrick, Emmons, & Larson, 2001). Since McCullough, Emmons, and Tsang's (2002) influential article was published, the clear conceptualization, definition, and measurement of dispositional gratitude has become available. Subsequently, scientific evidence has accumulated rapidly. These findings have indicated that gratitude reliably promotes an individual's well-being in areas such as life satisfaction and happiness (Chen & Kee, 2008; Froh, Charles, & Todd, 2009a; McCullough, Tsang, & Emmons, 2004; Wood, Joseph, & Maltby, 2008). It seems that the beneficial effect of gratitude is found across the board. However, as Gary and Cooper (2010) suggested, one successful way to improve theory is to delineate boundary conditions by examining the potential moderators. It is important to clarify when and where gratitude works best. To further advance knowledge about gratitude, we examine one of the potential moderators that may inhibit the beneficent effect of gratitude on wellbeing, specifically ambivalence over emotional expression.

Gratitude is a broad issue that can be investigated from multiple perspectives. For example, McCullough et al. (2002) defined gratitude as an affective trait—a "general tendency to recognize and respond with grateful emotion to the roles of other people's benevolence in the positive experiences and outcomes that one obtains" (p. 112). In this regard, individuals with high grateful traits are more likely to experience grateful moods and emotions in their social interactions. Wood, Froh, and Geraghty (2010) further conceptualized gratitude as a life orientation toward noticing and appreciating the positive in the world (p. 891). This definition is broader than McCullough et al's (2002) because it acknowledges fuller sources of gratitude, such as from nature or world events. However, we adhere to McCullough et al.'s original definition in this study because our research focuses more specifically on individuals' reactions to emotional dilemmas in their social encounters (such as receiving aid from another but hesitating to express thanks) than on people's general life orientation.

Following McCullough et al.'s (2002) definition, gratitude can be considered as a moral barometer that is sensitive to the changes of social relationships—the benefit received from another moral agent. McCullough et al. suggested that gratitude also induces individuals to behave prosocially to the benefactor or even to an unrelated third party. In addition, gratitude served as a moral reinforcement underlying reciprocal altruism. By simply saying ''thank you,'' the beneficiary substantiated the benefactor's benevolence and increased the possibility of receiving support from the benefactor in the future.

Fredrickson (2004) suggested that as gratitude fuels reciprocal altruism, which builds enduring friendship and social bonds, well-being can be enhanced through gratitude. This is because those social resources can be drawn upon when people face hardship in the future. Subsequently, research has found that gratitude reliably correlated with several well-being indexes. For example, Chen and Kee (2008) found gratitude negatively related to athlete burnout while having an inverse relationship with life satisfaction. In addition, gratitude was found to enhance outpatient well-being indexes (Toussaint & Friedman, 2009). Similarly, Vietnam War veterans benefited from being grateful (Kashdan, Uswatte, & Julian, 2006). Obviously, the psychological benefit of gratitude is reliable, and hence psychologists promote it.

Notwithstanding these findings, little is known about the boundary conditions, and this results in an obvious gap in knowledge. Since the importance of moderators for the value of long-term theory development should not be overlooked (Gary & Cooper, 2010), we direct our efforts to address this theoretical gap. One of the potential boundaries (moderators) constraining the beneficial effect of gratitude may be ambivalence over emotional expression, which is characterized as an interactional deficit in interpersonal relationships (Heisel & Mongrain, 2004). Individuals who are characterized by ambivalence over emotional expression either are inexpressive because they inhibit their desire to express, or are expressive but regret their expressiveness (King, 1998, p. 753). The concept is proposed to clarify the conflicts in the view that expressing emotion must be healthy, but inhibiting emotion undermines well-being. King and Emmons (1990) found that ambivalence over emotional expression negatively predicted life

satisfaction and predicted daily negative affect while it positively predicted depression and anxiety after controlling for emotional expressiveness. Subsequently, several similar findings have been reported (see Ben-Zur & Zimmerman, 2005; Emmons & Colby, 1995; Katz & Campbell, 1994; King & Emmons, 1991; Porter, Keefe, Lipkus, & Hurwitz, 2005; Tucker, Winkelman, Katz, & Bermas, 1999). Therefore, it is demonstrated that ambivalence over emotional expression is closely related to lower well-being rather than to expressiveness or inexpressiveness.
THE MODERATING ROLE OF AMBIVALENCE OVER EMOTIONAL EXPRESSION

This maladaption to interpersonal behaviors of ambivalence over emotional expression is the issue with which we are most concerned because it may inhibit the benefit of gratitude. We suggest that how ambivalence over emotional expression moderates the gratitude and well-being relationship might be understood from two perspectives. One is by misinterpreting social interaction, and the other is by displaying incongruent verbal and nonverbal behavior.

It is expected that when people receive help or benefit, they should acknowledge the benefactor to establish reciprocal altruism (McCullough et al., 2001). However, research indicates that ambivalent individuals might misinterpret the social situation (Emmons & Colby, 1995). For example, a beneficiary receives help but fails to be aware of or to acknowledge the benefactor, which results in a lower possibility of receiving help again. In this regard, the upward spirals of positive interaction would be interrupted even if they possessed the grateful trait. Evidence supporting our claim came from Emmons and Colby's (1995) study. They found that ambivalent individuals tend to perceive themselves as less likely to receive support from others. However, peer reports did not confirm this perception. In other words, ambivalent individuals tend to report less support from others even when their social network indeed does provide support.

Besides, ambivalent individuals may behave incongruently when they receive aid. Indirect research suggests that ambivalent individuals tend to have less congruency in verbal and nonverbal behavior during conflict resolution tasks (Heisel & Mongrain, 2004; Mongrain & Vettese, 2003). If this finding is also applicable to a positive emotional situation such as receiving gifts, one might imagine that grateful individuals with

high ambivalence over emotional expression might be less likely to display appropriate behavior in response to the benefactor such as smiling or saying ''thank you'' when receiving help. Therefore, we infer that the incongruent behavior may undermine the expected interpersonal interaction that is rooted in the script of gratitude. Support can also be found in the literature. For example, King's (1998) study found that ambivalent individuals tended to report opposite-valenced emotion words in reading emotional scenarios and facial expressions. In addition, ambivalent women were found to display a more constricted communication style and less congruency in their verbal and nonverbal communications during a conflict resolution task problem with their romantic partners (Mongrain & Vettese, 2003). A similar study indicated that ambivalence predicted a greater number of negative facial expressions and a briefer display of positive facial expressions (Heisel & Mongrain, 2004). Since the positive interpersonal interaction is one of the key components of gratitude to establish resources, the conflicts over incongruent expressiveness of gratitude might result in poor well-being.

In sum, the aim of the current study is to examine the potential moderating role of ambivalence over emotional expression on gratitude in a sample of Taiwanese college students. It was believed that we would discover under what specific conditions gratitude would not work best. This would be significant for both theory and practitioners. More specifically, we predicted that the relationship between gratitude and wellbeing would be inhibited under high ambivalence over emotional expression.

A total of 353 college students (male ¼ 108; female ¼ 245) with a mean age of 18.62 (SD ¼ .97) were recruited for this study. (Four students did not report their age.) A multisection questionnaire was administered to the participants in a quiet classroom setting. Constructs irrelevant to this study are not reported here. One of the authors was present to answer any queries raised by the participants. The participants took about 30 min to complete the entire set of questionnaires. Participants' involvement in this study was voluntary and their confidentiality as well as anonymity
was ensured. After completing the questionnaires, they were given a gift worth NT50.

Gratitude Questionnaire–Taiwan Version (GQ-T). The GQ was originally developed by McCullough et al. (2002) to measure disposition toward gratitude. Several studies in the West have demonstrated that the GQ is a psychometrically sound measurement (e.g., Froh et al., 2009a; Kashdan, Mishra, Breen, & Froh, 2009; Kashdan et al., 2006; Lambert, Fincham, Stillman, & Dean, 2009; Wood, Maltby, Gillett, Linley, & Joseph, 2008). Chen, Chen, Kee, and Tsai (2009) translated the GQ into Chinese, and the validity was supported by confirmatory factor analysis (CFA) in a study based on a sample of Taiwanese college students. It should be mentioned that one item (Long amounts of time can go by before I feel grateful to something or someone) was dropped due to the nonsignificant factor loading in CFA. Thus, the GQ-T contains five items designed to assess people's dispositional gratitude. Chen et al. (2009) reported that GQ-T positively correlated with theoretical constructs such as happiness, optimism, agreeableness, and extraversion. Chen and Kee (2008) also found GQ-T to be positively related to team satisfaction and life satisfaction, while a reverse relationship occurred with burnout in a sample of youth athletes in Taiwan. The two studies above indicated that the GQ-T possessed satisfactory reliability (Chen et al., 2009; Chen & Kee, 2008). In sum, the results supported the preliminary reliability and validity of the GQ-T. In the current study, participants indicated their responses on a seven-point Likert scale with responses ranging from strongly disagree (1) to strongly agree (7).

Ambivalence over Emotional Expression Questionnaire (AEQ). The AEQ is a 28-item scale developed by King and Emmons (1990) to measure conflict over one's emotional expressiveness. Emotional ambivalence includes ''wanting to express emotions and being unable to do so'' as well as ''expressing emotions and later regretting it.'' The AEQ has demonstrated satisfactory internal consistency and stability (King & Emmons, 1990), divergent and convergent validity (Katz & Campbell, 1994; King & Emmons, 1991), as well as external validity by observer ratings (Mongrain & Vettese, 2003).
For the sake of clarity and because we only considered the possible moderating role of ambivalence over emotional expression on the

relationship between gratitude and subjective happiness, several characteristics of AEQ might be inapplicable in this study. Therefore, we decided to exclude items containing negative emotional adjectives (e.g., anger, fear), specific positive emotional adjectives (e.g., love), and factor loading lower than .04 in order to reduce the ambiguity as well as interruption. By using the criteria described above, we finally selected the six items used to assess an individual's ambivalence over emotional expression. They were as follows: (1) Often I find that I am not able to tell others how much they really mean to me. (2) Often I'd like to show others how I feel, but something seems to be holding me back. (3) I want to express my emotions honestly but I am afraid that it may cause me embarrassment or hurt. (4) I often cannot bring myself to express what I am really feeling. (5) It is hard to find the right words to indicate to others what I am really feeling. (6) I would like to be more spontaneous in my emotional reactions but I just can't seem to do it. In the current study, participants indicated their responses on a seven-point Likert scale with responses ranging from do not agree (1) to agree (7).

The six-item AEQ was translated by a doctoral student majoring in social psychology who was proficient in both Chinese and English. After the AEQ was translated into Chinese, a second bilingual translator (English and Chinese) backtranslated the items into English. Both Chinese and English items were evaluated by the authors to ensure equivalence in meaning and comparability. Our pilot study1 involving another 235 college students revealed that the six-item AEQ positively related to the short-form UCLA Loneliness Scale (ULC-8) (r ¼ .48, p5.001; Wu & Yao, 2008) but was negatively correlated with Satisfaction with Life Scale–Chinese version (r ¼ -.21, p5.001; Wu & Yao, 2006) These relations provided preliminary evidence to support its criterion-related validity. The Cronbach's a was .87 in the pilot study.

In addition, we conducted a CFA for the current sample. The skewness and kurtosis for items range from -1 to 1; the Mardia kurtosis for multivariate normality statistics is 66.93. In order to account for the non-normality, a robust estimator with Satorra-Bentler scaled chi-square was used with LISREL 8.72. The Satorra-Bentler chi-squared value of this model was significant (SB-w2¼ 36.30, df ¼ 9, p5.05) because of the large sample size; however, various fit indices indicated that

this model is acceptable (TLI ¼ .97; CFI ¼ .98; RMSEA ¼ .09; SRMR ¼ .05). The overall model fit index satisfies the recommendations (Hu & Bentler, 1999). Based on the pilot and current data, therefore, we concluded that the six-item AEQ would be valid and reliable.

Subjective happiness. One item was used to assess participants' subjective happiness (e.g., On the whole, do you feel that you are having a happy life now?). This item was obtained from the Taiwan Social Change Survey (TSCS), which was supported by the National Science Council of Taiwan. This item was used in previous studies in Taiwan and was found to have a positive relation to marital status (Lee, 2007), income (Chiu, 2004), optimism, agreeableness, and extraversion; it had a negative correlation with neuroticism (Chen et al., 2009). Therefore, its purpose was to assess subjective happiness. Participants indicated their responses to this question on a seven-point Likert scale ranging from strongly disagree (1) to strongly agree (7).

The mean and standard deviation of variables are listed in Table 1. The Cronbach's a for both the gratitude and AEQ exceeded the recommendation of .70 (Nunnally & Bernstein, 1994). Gender was significantly correlated with gratitude (r ¼ .21, p5.001) and happiness (r ¼ .12, p5.05), suggesting that females are more grateful and happier. However, unexpectedly, we found a weak negative correlation between age and gratitude (r ¼ -.11, p5.05). Due to the significant correlations found, gender and age were included as control variables in our sequence analysis. As expected, the AEQ was negatively correlated with subjective happiness (r ¼ -.13, p5.05). On the other hand, gratitude was positively related to subjective happiness (r ¼ .31, p 5.05), but unrelated to AEQ score (r ¼ .02, ns). The pattern of correlation provided primary evidence to support our hypothesis.

These results corresponded to our expectation, and previous studies suggested that individuals who were high in dispositional gratitude experienced higher happiness, while AEQ undermined happiness (see Table 2). More importantly, the interaction was significant (B=-.17, p<.05) and accounted for an additional 2% of explained variance after controlling for the main effect. Although Study 1 primarily provided evidence to support the moderating role of ambivalence over emotional expression, two limitations would be further addressed in Study 2. First, the short version of AEQ was modified for the first time to examine the moderating effect, which causes the doubt that the moderation might be artificial. Therefore, we conducted Study 2 using the same scales with another independent student sample to cross-validated our findings from Study 1. Second, the single item used to assess overall subjective happiness in Study 1 might result in an incomplete understanding of well-being such as ignoring the negative indexes. Additional indexes including loneliness and depression were measured in Study 2 to address this limitation. By addressing the limitations, the authors could validate that the
moderating effect detected in Study 1 was not due to an idiosyncratic sample.

A total of 233 college students (male = 89; female = 144) with a mean age of 19.31 (SD = 2.10; one student did not report his age) were recruited for this study. One of the authors was present to answer any queries raised by the participants. The participants took about 30 min to complete the entire set of questionnaires. Participants' involvement in this study was voluntary and their confidentiality, as well as anonymity, was ensured.
The same scales of GQ-T, AEQ, and subjective happiness were used for Study 2.

Short form UCLA Loneliness Scale (ULS-8). The ULS-8 contains eight items selected from the revised UCLA Loneliness Scale (Hays & DiMatteo, 1987). This study employed a sevenpoint Likert scale ranging from strongly disagree (1) to strongly agree (7). The psychometrical properties of the ULC-8 had been examined with the Taiwanese sample (Wu & Yao, 2008). Their study demonstrated that the ULC-8 possessed satisfactory reliability and validity. The ULC-8 was also found to correlate negatively with life satisfaction and social support, but had a reverse relationship with anxiety and avoidant attachment. These were the sample statements: (1) "I can find companionship when I want it"; (2) "I am unhappy being so withdrawn"; and (3) "People are around me but not with me." The internal reliability of the ULS-8 was .78 in this study.

Center for Epidemiological Studies Depression Scale (CES-D). Symptoms of depression were measured by 20 items from the CES-D adapted for Chinese (Cheng & Chien, 1985). Sample items were "Don't feel like eating, bad appetite," and "Feeling sad and miserable." Respondents rated each item (symptom) on a five-point Likert scale ranging from never (0) to always (4). A higher total score indicated a higher level of depressive symptoms. In the present study, internal consistency alpha was .85 for this scale.

The mean, standard deviation and Cronbach's \alpha of variables are listed in Table 3. Gender correlated significantly with loneliness (r=-.13, p<.05) and gratitude (r=.13, p<.05). As expected, the AEQ was negatively correlated with subjective happiness (r=-.18, p<.01) but had a reverse relationship with loneliness (r=-.34, p<.001) and depression (r=-.51, p<.001). On the other hand, gratitude was positively related to subjective happiness (r=.46, p<.05) but had a reverse relationship with loneliness (r=-.49, p<.001) and depression (r=-.34, p<.001). The pattern of correlations provided primary evidence to support our hypothesis.

Both the gratitude and AEQ scores were standardized prior to the construction of the interaction terms, while subjective happiness, loneliness, and depression were left untransformed as in Study 1. However, the results did not support our expectation that ambivalence over emotional expression inhibited the positive effect of gratitude because the relationship between gratitude and loneliness was stronger for high ambivalence than for low ambivalence. A similar pattern was found for depression. Therefore, it was suggested that gratitude might have a strong protective effect to prevent illbeing.

As previous studies rarely explored the boundary conditions of gratitude, the aim of this study was to investigate the moderating role of ambivalence over emotional expression on the relationship between gratitude and well-being in a sample of Taiwanese students. Our results across two studies indicated that grateful individuals tend to be healthy, while those who are ambivalent over emotional expression do not. More importantly, a significant moderating effect was found, and the results partially corresponded to our expectation. We found that ambivalence inhibited the relationship between gratitude and subjective happiness across two studies. However, the inhibited effect was not supported for the relationship between gratitude and illbeing indexes (loneliness and depression) because the relationships were stronger for high ambivalence than for low ambivalence.
The effect of gratitude and ambivalence over emotional expression on well-being

For the beneficial effect of gratitude on well-being, researchers indicated that seeing oneself as the beneficiary of other people's generosity may allow one to feel valued, loved, and supported. Also, grateful people are motivated to be prosocial to the benefactor or third party (McCullough et al., 2001, 2002). The reciprocal altruism would chronically develop into social resources on which one could draw in the future (Fredrickson, 2004). This seems to help grateful people to enhance or maintain their well-being. Our finding corresponds to a number of studies in the literature (e.g., Chen et al., 2009; Chen & Kee, 2008; Emmons & McCullough, 2003; Froh et al., 2009a; Wood et al., 2008a, 2008b).
Another important finding is the main effect of ambivalence over emotional expression, which

negatively predicted happiness but has a reverse relationship with loneliness and depression. It is suggested that when ambivalent people are stuck in an approach–avoidance conflict regarding whether to express their emotions or express them only with regret, this would result in a negative mood state (Mongrain & Vettese, 2003). Tucker et al. (1999) also suggested that ambivalent individuals may adapt ineffective coping strategies to deal with stress, such as distancing themselves emotionally from the situation or blaming themselves or others. In addition, research indicated that ambivalent individuals may have negative biases in interpreting others' supportive behavior (Emmons & Colby, 1995), which is receiving support from others while not feeling satisfied with it. Those facets of ambivalence over emotional expression seem to lead ambivalent people to be more lonely, depressed, and unhappy, an outcome that is compatible with previous studies (Ben-Zur & Zimmerman, 2005; Katz & Campbell, 1994; King & Emmons, 1990, 1991; Tucker et al., 1999).
The inhibiting effect of ambivalence over emotional expression

The most important finding in this study is that ambivalence over emotional expression moderated the relationship between gratitude and well-being indexes. This could be considered a significant contribution to the literature. The significant moderation for subjective happiness (in both Study 1 and Study 2) reminds us that positive life events need to be handled appropriately (Katz & Campbell, 1994), especially when individuals are inhibiting their desire to express or regretting their expressiveness. Fredrickson's (2004) theory emphasizes the role of positive emotion in determining individuals' well-being. The moderation contributes to her theory by providing a platform to highlight the importance of the discovery of the boundaries of positive emotions.

It is obvious that gratitude does not work under the condition of high ambivalence over emotional expression. There are two possible explanations for this moderation. One is cognitive bias in reading social interaction; the other is incongruent behavior. King (1998) inferred that ambivalent people might have some kind of cognitive bias in interpreting emotion even if their perceptions are accurate. They tend to ''read too much emotion'' even in simple emotional situations, which leads them to mistrust the expressions of others. Furthermore, when receiving help from others,

ambivalent people tend to be less able to interpret the situation accurately, and may not respond to the benefactor appropriately even when they are grateful. Certainly, research found that ambivalent women participating in conflict resolution tasks displayed less verbal behavior accompanied by matching nonverbal behavior (Mongrain & Vettese, 2003). This provides indirect evidence to support our inference. Thus, the reciprocal altruism rooted in gratitude might be attributed, and the social resources could not be cultivated.

Interestingly, although the moderation was significant, the inhibited effect was not supported for the relationship between gratitude and illbeing indexes (both loneliness and depression). In Figures 3 and 4, one can observe that the slopes of low ambivalence over emotional expression were flatter than high ambivalence over emotional expression. The patterns of loneliness and depression are contrary to the result of subjective happiness. This might imply that high gratitude has a strong protective effect against illbeing, regardless of the high or low ambivalence over emotional expression. The high level of loneliness and depression are experienced when low gratitude is accompanied by high ambivalence. However, the asymmetric patterns will require further investigation to clarify the boundary conditions of gratitude. In sum, the findings from the two studies provide us robust evidence to delineate boundary conditions of gratitude.

Readers might have doubt about the existence of moderation perhaps being due to the deliberate selection of items. However, as we observed, the short-form AEQ correlated consistently with theoretically related constructs across three independent samples (the pilot study, Study 1, and Study 2), suggesting that its validity is supported. Besides, the reliability across studies is satisfactory (Cronbach's a ranged from .85 to .87). In addition, the results of our two studies provide further evidence that the moderation is not due to an idiosyncratic sample. Therefore, both the shortform AEQ and moderation should be considered as valid. The use of multiple well-being indexes in our studies also further provided us with a complete picture to understand the moderating effect of ambivalence over emotional expression. Those findings contain valuable information to design intervention, which is discussed below.

The most important application drawn from this current study might be the asymmetric patterns of moderation. Our findings suggested that the psychological benefit of gratitude is more likely to prevent individuals from suffering illbeing than to promote willbeing. If this were true, gratitude intervention that targets a promotion of well-being needs to be carefully designed, such as by including potential moderators that may interfere with the effectiveness. Our suggestion corresponds to Froh et al.'s (2009b) appeal to investigate whether certain people are more inclined to derive benefit from gratitude intervention (p. 410). Using our study as an example, the better question may become, who does not derive benefit from gratitude intervention? Obviously, the answer is that ambivalent people are less likely to benefit from gratitude intervention. Therefore, the effect of gratitude intervention would be enhanced and clarified by identifying the moderator.

In addition, our study identified that ambivalence over emotional expression is a moderator. To reduce ambivalence is also an important issue for practitioners. To the authors' knowledge, only one study has made a direct effort to deal with this issue. Chang et al. (2010) used psychological displacement writing (PDW) as their intervention. They had participants write in their diaries sequentially using first-person, second-person, and third-person pronouns, and the results indicated that ambivalence over emotional expression would be reduced. Although ambivalence over emotional expression is generally considered as an individual differences construct (King & Emmons, 1990), Chang et al.'s (2010) study suggests that PDW might be an efficient way to reduce people's ambivalence. Future study could explore diverse interventions aimed at reducing emotional ambivalence.

Limitations should be addressed when interpreting the current results. First, all the measurements are self-reported and collected at the same time. There is a common method variance, which might inflate the relationships between variables and further threaten internal validity (Lindell & Whitney, 2001). It might be possible to conduct multiple methods as a way to overcome this shortcoming. Second, ambivalence over emotional expression was measured by six items extracted from the original scale. We admit that this would narrow the scope of ambivalence over emotional expression, and results should be interpreted with caution. However, the items used in this study might be appropriate because they tap the meaning

of ambivalence over emotional expression, which is most closely related to our research, and they demonstrated satisfactory validity and reliability. Third, the explained variance for the interaction seems quite small for both Study 1 and Study 2. However, as Chaplin (1991) suggested, interactive effects are difficult to detect in field-based work, and they seldom contribute more than 3% of explained variance. The explained variance in the current study seems acceptable, but future study should use multiple methods to replicate and extend current findings. Since studies are rarely conducted to delineate the boundary conditions of gratitude, the current study advances our knowledge about gratitude.

In past decades, the increase in gratitude research received much attention from psychologists. Although studies demonstrate that gratitude is beneficial for people's well-being, little is known about the boundary conditions of gratitude. Our studies represent an initial attempt to clarify the boundaries. The studies underscore the importance of emotional ambivalence in people's social lives. The beneficial effect of gratitude may not work well when individuals are stuck in an approach/ avoid conflict. The current study also highlights the need for further exploration in the area of gratitude-related research.
